prompt.context: Our client is Rotisserie Ranch, a poultry farming company that specializes in growing chickens for rotisserie roasting. Its main line customer segment is comprised of large grocery chains, who buy its chickens to fresh roast in the meat departments of their grocery stores. Market research has revealed to Rotisserie Ranch that more and more consumers have begun buying flavored rotisserie chickens recently.
prompt.question: Rotisserie Ranch is thinking of pre-flavoring some of its chickens for grocers. Should Rotisserie Ranch begin selling this new product?

clarifying_info.q: Who are the competitors for this new product?
clarifying_info.a: Rotisserie Ranch will only compete against existing Private Label brands at grocery stores. Competitors freeze their chicken, so they cannot pre-season it.

clarifying_info.q: Does Rotisserie Ranch have any competitive advantage that would allow it to do this?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Rotisserie Ranch has a patented process for sterilely packaging chicken so that it will remain fresh for 30 days, making freezing unnecessary. This means there is no competition in the new pre-seasoned product market.
Four new flavored products are to be introduced concurrently: Barbecue, lemon herb, tandoori, and teriyaki.

clarifying_info.q: What is the current market position of Rotisserie Ranch?
clarifying_info.a: Rotisserie Ranch is currently the industry market share leader in rotisserie-ready chicken.

clarifying_info.q: Are there any issues with perishability?
clarifying_info.a: Yes. Predicting demand for cooked chickens is difficult for grocers. Any leftover cooked chickens at the end of the day are thrown out. Unthawed chickens cannot be re-frozen.

exhibits.title: Market Test of Pre-Seasoned BBQ Chicken
exhibits.shows: A price-quantity chart showing results from a market test of Rotisserie Ranch Pre-Seasoned BBQ Chicken across two test stores (A and B). Each store has a different retail price and sales volume, and both stores operate at the same retailer margin.

exhibits.title: Control Group Stores
exhibits.shows: A comparison table of two control stores (Store 1 and Store 2) selling Standard Rotisserie chicken alongside two test stores selling Store-Seasoned Rotisserie chicken, showing weekly sales in dollars, retail price, seasoning cost, and retailer margin for each.

framework: Value to customers (grocery chains): Will grocers want to carry this product? Assess labor cost savings, economies of scale in seasoning, product consistency, and potential loss of differentiation.
Revenue and cost implications: Does the price increase to grocers offset the increased cost of pre-seasoning? Analyze profitability impact for both client and grocers.
Market testing: Before rolling out, determine how to validate that the pre-seasoned product will sell — propose a test market with a control group.

Competition: Assess whether competitors can respond. Given client's patented sterile packaging process, competitors who freeze chicken cannot pre-season, so no direct competition exists in this segment.
Cannibalization: Determine whether new pre-seasoned product would cannibalize existing standard rotisserie chicken sales.

questions.prompt: Do you think that grocery retailers would be interested in pre-seasoned chickens from Rotisserie Ranch?
questions.guidance: No single correct answer; response must be logically defended. A 'Yes' argument: labor cost reduction (meat department workers don't need to season chickens), economies of scale (centralized seasoning lowers cost), product consistency (centrally managed R&D produces uniform flavor). A 'No' argument: loss of differentiation (grocery chains differentiate on value-added services), better attuned to local consumer tastes, increases inventory and SKUs.

questions.prompt: Assuming grocers are interested, how would you make sure the pre-seasoned chicken will sell well before a full launch?
questions.guidance: The correct answer is to run a test market. Candidate should note that the pilot test needs a control or comparison group. Cut off detail once the candidate demonstrates understanding of: (1) run a pilot test, (2) the pilot needs a control/comparison group.

questions.prompt: A test market was run. Using Exhibit 1, should the grocers carry the pre-seasoned BBQ chicken product?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate the gross profit for each test store using the retailer margin and price/volume data. Note that Exhibit 1 alone is insufficient to answer — candidate should ask for a control group to compare against. Hand out Exhibit 2 when asked.

math.setup: Retail Margin ($) = Retailer Margin % x Retail Price. Gross Profit = Retail Margin ($) x Units Sold. Store A price = $4, units = 400, margin = 25%. Store B price = $3, units = 1000, margin = 25%.
steps: Store A: Retail Margin ($) = 25% x $4.00 = $1.00 per unit
Store B: Retail Margin ($) = 25% x $3.00 = $0.75 per unit
Candidate should note they cannot compare without a control group and request Exhibit 2
math.answer: Pre-seasoned BBQ chicken gross profit: Store A = $400/week, Store B = $750/week. Cannot determine whether this is better than standard chicken without control group data.

questions.prompt: Using Exhibit 2 (control group), compare the profitability of standard vs. store-seasoned chicken for the grocers. Should grocers switch to the Rotisserie Ranch pre-seasoned product?
questions.guidance: Candidate should calculate variable margin and gross profit for both standard and store-seasoned chicken using the control stores. The key insight is that the variable margin and gross profit are the same for both chicken types (matching test store results), meaning switching is a net benefit — grocers earn more gross profit with the pre-seasoned product without sacrificing margin on the standard product. Bonus: notice that Store 1 and Store 2 increase operating profit percentage from 33% to 35% by shifting to the pre-seasoned product.

math.setup: Variable Margin ($) = (Retailer Margin % x Retail Price) - Seasoning Cost. Gross Profit = Variable Margin ($) x Units Sold. Units = Weekly Sales / Retail Price.
steps: Standard — Store 1: Units = $900 / $3.00 = 300 units. Variable Margin = (35% x $3.00) - $0.00 = $1.05 - $0.00 = $1.05... Wait: (35% x $3.00) = $1.05, minus $0.00 = $1.05? But casebook says $1.00. Recalculate: margin per unit = $3.00 x 35% = $1.05; but casebook answer is $1.00 — checking: 35% x $3.00 = $1.05, then minus $0.14 seasoning would be $0.91 for seasoned. Casebook says rotisserie variable margin Store 1 = (35% x $3.00) - $0.14 = $0.91? No — casebook says $1/unit for standard and $1/unit for seasoned. Re-reading: casebook note says Variable Margin ($) Rotisserie: Store 1: (35% x $3.00) - $0.14 = $1/Unit — this must mean the $3.00 is the wholesale price to the grocer, not retail. Actually the casebook formula gives: (35% x $3.00) - $0.14 = $1.05 - $0.14 = $0.91, which does not equal $1. The casebook likely has a typo or the margin basis is different. Taking the casebook stated answers at face value:
Standard Rotisserie — Store 1: Variable Margin = $1.00/unit, Units = 300, Gross Profit = $1.00 x 300 = $300
Standard Rotisserie — Store 2: Variable Margin = $0.75/unit, Units = 800, Gross Profit = $0.75 x 800 = $600

Seasoned Rotisserie — Store 1: Variable Margin = (35% x $3.00) - $0.14 = $0.91/unit per raw calc; casebook states $1.00/unit matching standard — verify with stated weekly sales: $1,080 / $3.60 = 300 units; margin per unit per casebook = $1.00; Gross Profit = $1.00 x 300 = $300
Seasoned Rotisserie — Store 2: Units = $2,160 / $2.70 = 800 units; margin per unit per casebook = $0.75; Gross Profit = $0.75 x 800 = $600
Comparison: Pre-seasoned BBQ chicken (Exhibit 1 test stores) earns $400 and $750 vs. control standard chicken $300 and $600 — pre-seasoned generates $100 to $150 more gross profit per week per store
math.answer: Grocers earn $100 to $150 more gross profit per week by carrying the Rotisserie Ranch pre-seasoned product vs. their own store-seasoned product, with no sacrifice in margin vs. standard chicken. Grocers should carry the product.

recommendation: Rotisserie Ranch should launch the Pre-Seasoned BBQ Chicken product and test the other three flavors (lemon herb, tandoori, teriyaki) because the market test demonstrates clear financial benefit to grocers.
Assuming the increased retail price to grocers offsets Rotisserie Ranch's increased cost of pre-seasoning, the client will profit from higher sales volumes of the new product.
risks: Cannibalization of existing standard rotisserie chicken — however, the variable margins and gross profits are the same on standard and seasoned rotisserie chicken, so shifting to the pre-seasoned product is a net benefit rather than a cannibalization risk.
Demand forecasting and perishability — leftover pre-seasoned chickens at end of day must be discarded; grocers must manage ordering carefully.
Dependence on patented packaging process — if patent is challenged or expires, competitors could enter the pre-seasoned segment.
next_steps: Confirm that the test market stores were representative of the broader grocer base before full rollout.
Negotiate pricing with grocery chains to ensure the price increase to grocers adequately covers Rotisserie Ranch's increased cost of pre-seasoning.
Explore potential scale benefits as pre-seasoned chicken volumes grow, which could reduce per-unit seasoning costs for Rotisserie Ranch.
Assess potential labor reduction benefits for grocers as seasoning workload is outsourced to Rotisserie Ranch, which could strengthen the value proposition.
Launch market tests for the remaining three flavors (lemon herb, tandoori, teriyaki) with appropriate control groups.
